title: Trigonometry essentials
note: On the unit circle, the point at angle θ is (cos θ, sin θ), so cos is the x-coordinate and sin is the y-coordinate. Memorize the first-quadrant values at π/6, π/4, and π/3; signs elsewhere follow from the quadrant. Most identities grow out of sin²θ + cos²θ = 1.

read.title: Why the unit circle is enough
text: Draw a circle of radius 1 centered at the origin. Starting from the point (1, 0), walk counterclockwise along the circle a distance θ. Because the radius is 1, that arc length is also the angle in radians. The point where you stop has coordinates (cos θ, sin θ). That is the definition: cosine is the x-coordinate and sine is the y-coordinate.

Several facts fall out immediately. Every point on the circle satisfies x² + y² = 1, so sin²θ + cos²θ = 1. Both coordinates stay between −1 and 1, which is the range of sine and cosine. A full trip around is 2π, so both functions repeat with period 2π. Reflecting an angle across the x-axis turns θ into −θ, keeps x, and flips y, so cos(−θ) = cos θ while sin(−θ) = −sin θ.

You only need to memorize three first-quadrant angles. At π/6 the point is (√3/2, 1/2); at π/4 it is (√2/2, √2/2); at π/3 it is (1/2, √3/2). Any other standard angle has the same coordinates up to sign, and the quadrant tells you which signs apply. For example, 5π/6 lies in the second quadrant, where x is negative, so cos(5π/6) = −√3/2.

q.q: On the unit circle, sin θ is which coordinate of the point at angle θ?

o: Every point on the unit circle satisfies x² + y² = 1
5π/6 is in the second quadrant, where x < 0
